workedExamples.title: The vertical-line test: does the graph show a function?

steps.prompt: A relation is a function when every input (x-value) is paired with exactly one output (y-value). On a graph, the vertical-line test checks this. What does a vertical line represent?
steps.reveal: A vertical line is the set of all points that share one single x-value. Sliding it left and right lets you check, one input at a time, how many outputs that input has.

steps.prompt: Picture the graph of a sideways parabola opening to the right (like x = y²). Sweep a vertical line across it. At x = 4, how many points does the line touch?
steps.reveal: Two points: (4, 2) and (4, −2). The single input x = 4 is paired with two outputs, 2 and −2.

steps.prompt: State the rule for the vertical-line test based on what you just saw.
steps.reveal: If ANY vertical line crosses the graph more than once, the relation is NOT a function. If every possible vertical line hits the graph at most once, it IS a function.

steps.prompt: So is the sideways parabola a function? And what is the common reading mistake?
steps.reveal: It is NOT a function, because the vertical line at x = 4 hits twice. The classic mistake is reading the test horizontally or only checking a spot where the line happens to hit once — you must be able to find even one vertical line that hits twice to disqualify it.

steps.prompt: Now consider an upward parabola, y = x². Apply the same sweep. Function or not?
steps.reveal: Every vertical line hits y = x² exactly once, so it IS a function. Many inputs (like x = 2 and x = −2) share the output 4 — that is allowed. A function only forbids one input giving two outputs, never two inputs sharing one output.

workedExamples.title: Function vs. one-to-one: don't conflate them

steps.prompt: Look at the relation {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)}. Is each input paired with exactly one output?
steps.reveal: Yes. Input 1 → 5, input 2 → 5, input 3 → 9. Every input has exactly one output, so this IS a function.

steps.prompt: Inputs 1 and 2 both map to output 5. Does that break the function rule?
steps.reveal: No. The function rule only restricts OUTPUTS per input — each input may have just one output. Two different inputs sharing the same output is completely allowed. This is called many-to-one.

steps.prompt: A function is one-to-one when, in addition to being a function, every output also comes from exactly one input. Is {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)} one-to-one?
steps.reveal: No. The output 5 is produced by two inputs, 1 and 2. So it is a function but NOT one-to-one.
Function: yes, each input has one output. One-to-one: yes, each output (5, 7, 9) traces back to exactly one input. So this is a function AND one-to-one.

steps.prompt: Why is it wrong to call {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)} 'not a function'?
steps.reveal: Calling it 'not a function' confuses the one-to-one condition with the function condition. Repeated OUTPUTS never disqualify a function; only a repeated INPUT with differing outputs does. Many-to-one relations are valid functions — they just are not one-to-one.
